desc:
In the m x n matrix grid, each row is sorted in non-decreasing order, and the first value of every row is greater than or equal to the last value of the row above it. Reading the cells row by row therefore gives one long non-decreasing sequence of m * n values.

Return the position (0-based, in that row-by-row order) where target would have to be inserted to keep the sequence sorted, placing it before any equal values. Equivalently, return how many cells hold a value strictly smaller than target. The answer lies between 0 and m * n.
constraints: Reading the grid row by row gives a non-decreasing sequence
hints: Scanning counts the smaller cells in O(m * n). The row-by-row order is sorted, which is exactly what binary search needs.
Treat the grid as one array of length m * n. Position p of that array lives at row p // n, column p % n.
Binary search for the first position p whose value is ≥ target, with search range [0, m * n] (the upper end means 'all values are smaller'). Compare grid[p // n][p % n] with the target.
editorial: Because each row begins at or after the previous row's end, the cells read row by row form a sorted array, and you can binary search it without building it: position p corresponds to grid[p // n][p % n].

We want the lower bound: the smallest p with value ≥ target, or m * n if there is none. Keep lo = 0 and hi = m * n; while lo < hi take mid, and if the cell at mid is smaller than the target move lo = mid + 1, otherwise hi = mid. The result is lo.

The loop runs about log<sub>2</sub>(m * n) times, so the time is O(log(m * n)) with O(1) space. Searching for the first position with value ≥ target (rather than any equal value) is what makes the answer unique when the grid has duplicates.
